stem: An MCP integration must let an IDE attach a database schema whenever a project opens, without waiting for the model to request it. During a conversation, the model may separately request an approved record update. Which interface design best separates application-selected context from model-requested operations?

options.text: Expose schemas as resources the IDE can read and attach, and expose record updates as tools subject to execution approval.
Expose schemas through a user-invoked prompt template, and expose record updates as tools subject to execution approval.
Expose schema lookup and record updates as tools, and let the model decide when the schema should enter the conversation.
Expose schemas as resources the IDE can attach, and represent each update as a resource the IDE reads to apply the change.

explanation: Resources provide application-driven access to contextual data, including database schemas. The IDE can read and attach a schema independently of a model tool call. Tools expose operations that the model can request, with host approval where appropriate. A prompt template is user-invoked, while reading a resource is not the interface for a record mutation.

distractorNotes.b: A user-invoked template can package context, but it does not meet the automatic project-open attachment requirement.
distractorNotes.c: A schema lookup tool is a viable interface for model-driven discovery, but this design makes attachment depend on a model decision.
distractorNotes.d: Resources expose read-only context; a state-changing update belongs behind an executable tool rather than a resource read.

sourceNote: Core Server Features / Resources, Tools and Prompts interaction models

stem: A build-artifact inventory agent uses the Agent SDK. Its MCP server exposes listing tools and a delete_artifact tool, but deletion is outside this agent's role. Developers have listed the read tools in allowedTools and assumed deletion is now unavailable. A trace still shows deletion proposals awaiting approval. The server is shared with legitimate cleanup jobs. Which change removes the unwanted capability from this agent without changing the shared server?

options.text: Keep the read-tool allow rules and use a non-interactive permission mode to reject deletion requests that would require approval.
Deny the deletion tool by its full bare tool name in this agent's configuration so its definition is removed from model context.
Keep the read-tool allow rules and add a permission callback that denies each proposed deletion before the server receives it.
Defer the deletion tool's definition behind tool search, retaining it in the catalog in case future inventory requests need it.

explanation: The Agent SDK's allow list pre-approves listed tools; it does not remove unlisted tools. A bare-name deny entry removes that tool definition from the request, preventing the agent from proposing it through that interface while leaving the shared server unchanged. Approval-time denial and deferred discovery serve different purposes: neither removes the unnecessary capability from this agent's available toolset.

distractorNotes.a: Rejecting approval-requiring calls can prevent execution, but the definition remains available and the agent can still propose deletion.
distractorNotes.c: A callback can deny a call that reaches it, but the requirement is to remove the capability rather than repeatedly evaluate proposals.
distractorNotes.d: Tool search reduces initial context load, not authorization scope; the deferred deletion tool remains discoverable.

sourceNote: Allow and deny rules / Bare-name deny removes tool definitions; allow rules pre-approve

stem: A platform exposes 95 microservice tools. Cached requests are cheaper, but the model still confuses similar operations and reads 50,000 tokens of definitions. Requests often span several services, so routing each request to one service would lose required capabilities. The team can accept an extra discovery step. Which design best reduces active schema volume while retaining cross-service reach?

options.text: Keep the complete tool catalog loaded, cache its stable prefix, and improve descriptions to distinguish similar operations.
Route each request to a service-specific agent with a small toolset, and keep the request inside that service for its duration.
Keep common tools loaded and defer the remaining catalog behind tool search, loading relevant definitions as work crosses services.
Expose a generic service dispatcher and include the complete endpoint and argument catalog in its description for model selection.

explanation: Tool search addresses both context bloat and selection difficulty by loading deferred definitions when needed. Keeping frequently used tools loaded avoids unnecessary discovery for common operations, while the searchable catalog preserves access across services. Caching the full catalog reduces repeated-prefix processing cost but does not remove its definitions from the model's active context. Discovery adds work, so the scenario explicitly permits that latency trade-off.

distractorNotes.a: Better descriptions can help selection, but this retains the active schema volume that caching has already failed to address.
distractorNotes.b: A service-specific toolset reduces context, but confinement to one service violates the cross-service task requirement.
distractorNotes.d: Combining names into one dispatcher does not reduce definition volume when its description still carries the full endpoint catalog.

sourceNote: Tool search tool / Context bloat and tool selection accuracy scaling

stem: A local financial-data MCP server uses Streamable HTTP, binds to loopback, and authenticates its approved desktop client. A browser-based attack test sends requests with an untrusted Origin after DNS rebinding. The team must retain the HTTP integration. Which change addresses the missing transport control without treating authentication or local binding as substitutes?

options.text: Validate incoming Origin headers and reject present invalid origins with HTTP 403, retaining loopback binding and authentication.
Rotate the client's authentication credentials more frequently and retain the existing acceptance policy for incoming Origin headers.
Enforce Origin checks on tool execution requests, but exempt discovery and resource requests because they do not modify financial data.
Reject requests to non-loopback addresses and rely on that destination check to distinguish approved clients from browser-based callers.

explanation: Streamable HTTP requires Origin validation on incoming connections and HTTP 403 when a present Origin is invalid. The specification separately recommends loopback binding for local servers and proper authentication. Those existing controls do not replace the mandated Origin check, and the check is not limited to mutating tool requests.

distractorNotes.b: Credential rotation maintains authentication hygiene but does not implement the missing Origin-validation requirement.
distractorNotes.c: The transport requirement applies to incoming connections, not merely requests that modify records.
distractorNotes.d: Loopback limits network exposure, but the specification explicitly warns about remote websites reaching local servers through DNS rebinding.

sourceNote: Streamable HTTP / Security & Endpoint (Origin validation, localhost binding, authentication)

stem: A filing-extraction pipeline uses Claude Sonnet 5 without manual extended thinking. Its request includes lookup and record_filing_entity tools, but this stage requires a call to record_filing_entity rather than a lookup or conversational answer. The supported input schema uses required string and number fields, with no enum, const, or value-range constraints. Refused or truncated responses are handled separately. Which design enforces the intended operation and field structure for a completed tool call?

options.text: Use strict schemas for the provided tools with automatic tool choice, and instruct the model to prefer the recording operation.
Request a schema-constrained JSON response without tool use, then have the application dispatch that response to the recording service.
Require a tool call from the registered set and use strict schemas, allowing the model to choose the operation from the filing content.
Force record_filing_entity with tool_choice and enable strict: true on its definition to constrain the generated arguments to its schema.

explanation: Specific tool choice fixes the operation; strict tool use constrains the completed call to the supported schema's required fields and types. Neither requirement implies the other. Structured JSON output is an alternative integration design, but it does not produce the required model tool call. The explicitly supported model and thinking configuration allow forced tool choice. This claim is limited to the stated field structure and separately handled refusal or truncation cases, not arbitrary schema constraints or the factual correctness of extracted values.

distractorNotes.a: Strictness governs arguments if a tool is called; automatic choice still permits another tool or a conversational response.
distractorNotes.b: Structured output can satisfy a JSON contract, but application dispatch is not the required model-generated tool invocation.
distractorNotes.c: Requiring some tool with strict arguments still permits a lookup instead of the recording operation.

sourceNote: Define tools / Forcing tool use and Strict tool use

stem: An inventory agent's application already rejects reservations unless a fresh stock check has succeeded. Separately, its tool runner accepts at most one proposed call per model turn; Claude currently emits stock-check and reservation calls together. Both tools should remain available, and conversational answers should remain possible. Which request policy satisfies that narrower turn-shape contract?

options.text: Allow parallel proposals but execute their tool calls sequentially in the application before returning results to Claude.
Use automatic tool choice with disable_parallel_tool_use: true, while retaining the application's reservation prerequisite check.
Force the stock-check tool on each request and let the existing reservation prerequisite check decide whether its result is fresh.
Retain automatic parallel tool choice and describe the runner's one-call limit in the system prompt and both tool descriptions.

explanation: With automatic tool choice, disabling parallel tool use limits a response to at most one tool call while still permitting a text-only answer. This controls the number of proposed calls, not which call comes first. The application must retain its existing stock-check prerequisite enforcement: a one-call response could still propose reservation before a successful check.

distractorNotes.a: Sequential execution does not change the response shape; the runner would still receive multiple proposed calls in one turn.
distractorNotes.c: Forcing stock checks prevents the required freedom to propose reservations or answer conversationally on appropriate turns.
distractorNotes.d: Instructions can encourage fewer calls but do not enforce the API-level at-most-one-call constraint.

sourceNote: Parallel tool use / Execution semantics and Disabling parallel tool use

stem: A Messages API client successfully receives a SQL tool call, but executing the read-only query times out. The application has recorded the failure in its trace and exhausted its permitted backend retries. Claude should now decide whether to narrow the query or explain the failure, with the original call accounted for in conversation history. Which response design fits?

options.text: Retry the original model request as an API transport failure, leaving the timed-out tool call out of the next conversation.
Return a successful empty-row tool result and keep the timeout details in traces so downstream processing retains its normal shape.
Return a matching tool_result with is_error: true and a timeout explanation, preserving the distinction between failure and empty data.
Append a user message describing the timeout instead of a tool result, allowing the model to read the failure in natural language.

explanation: Client-tool execution errors can be returned in a user message as a tool_result matching the original tool_use_id, with is_error: true and informative content. This closes the outstanding tool call and gives Claude evidence for recovery. A successful Messages API response followed by a backend timeout is not itself a Messages API transport failure, and an empty successful query result would misrepresent what happened.

distractorNotes.a: Regenerating the model request does not communicate the known execution failure to the existing conversation.
distractorNotes.b: A timeout establishes neither a successful query nor absence of rows; traces alone do not give that distinction to Claude.
distractorNotes.d: Natural-language content belongs inside the matching tool result; a standalone user message leaves the tool call unanswered.

sourceNote: Handle tool calls / Handling results from client tools / is_error

stem: A policy RAG system retrieves 400-token chunks. A reimbursement clause is repeatedly missed because its division and employee grade appear elsewhere in the manual, not in the indexed chunk. The generation prompt has a strict size budget, and the retriever must identify the right clause before fetching larger parent sections. Which indexing change best addresses the observed failure?

options.text: Prepend concise chunk-specific context derived from the full document before creating both embeddings and lexical index entries.
Index a generic summary of each manual alongside its chunks, using the same summary text to represent each clause's applicability.
Keep the existing chunk index and attach a larger parent section after retrieval so the generator can resolve each clause's scope.
Keep the existing chunk index and increase the retrieved chunk count until distant division and grade headings reach the generator.

explanation: Contextual Retrieval adds concise, chunk-specific explanatory context before embedding and BM25 indexing. The retriever can then match qualifiers that were absent from the isolated clause. This targets candidate selection rather than hoping the generator can repair missing context after retrieval. The source distinguishes this method from generic document summaries and recommends evaluating chunking and retrieval settings on the actual use case.

distractorNotes.b: A shared document summary does not distinguish the applicability of individual clauses; the method uses context specific to each chunk.
distractorNotes.c: Parent expansion can help interpret a retrieved clause, but this failure occurs before the correct child chunk is selected.
distractorNotes.d: Increasing retrieved context pressures the stated prompt budget and leaves the missing qualifiers absent from the indexed clause.

sourceNote: Introducing Contextual Retrieval / The context conundrum in traditional RAG

stem: A field engineering knowledge base contains narrative troubleshooting procedures and exact hardware identifiers such as PN-7740-X. Queries often combine both. Vector search performs well on procedures but misses exact part numbers. The team can afford an extra ranking stage but cannot increase the final context budget. Which pipeline best addresses both query signals while selecting a limited set of relevant chunks?

options.text: Use dense embeddings with a larger final top-k, relying on the generation model to find exact identifiers in the additional context.
Use contextual BM25 with reranking, replacing the semantic retriever so exact hardware identifiers determine the candidate pool.
Deploy an intent classification model ahead of the retriever to route queries exclusively to either vector search or BM25.
Combine contextual embeddings with contextual BM25 using rank fusion, and pass the top candidate chunks through a reranker.

explanation: The source combines semantic embeddings with BM25's lexical matching, merges candidates using rank fusion, and reranks them before selecting the final context. This retains both signals for mixed queries without requiring a larger final chunk set. Reranking adds runtime cost and latency, which the scenario permits; the research results support testing this combination, not a guarantee that it is best for every corpus.

distractorNotes.a: This retains the observed identifier-retrieval weakness and increases final context despite the fixed budget.
distractorNotes.b: BM25 helps exact matching but discards the semantic signal that already works for narrative procedures; reranking cannot recover absent candidates.
distractorNotes.c: Classifier routing forces an all-or-nothing choice, whereas technical queries (e.g. troubleshooting a specific part number) benefit from both dense semantic and sparse lexical signals fused together.

sourceNote: A primer on RAG / Further boosting performance with Reranking

stem: Two new MCP integrations target revision 2026-07-28. For A, the host launches and owns a local repository-inspection subprocess; policy prohibits opening a listening socket. For B, an independently operated Kubernetes service must accept requests from many remote clients without those clients launching server processes. Which transport pairing fits both lifecycle and connectivity constraints?

options.text: Use loopback Streamable HTTP for A to retain an HTTP interface, and network Streamable HTTP for B to share the remote service.
Use stdio over the host-owned subprocess streams for A, and Streamable HTTP to reach the independently operated service for B.
Use stdio over the host-owned subprocess streams for A, and the deprecated HTTP+SSE transport for B as the default for new clients.
Use stdio for A and launch a separate remote server subprocess through SSH for each B client rather than sharing its service endpoint.

explanation: The standard transports fit different process relationships: stdio carries messages over a client-launched subprocess's streams, while Streamable HTTP serves independently operated network endpoints. A explicitly requires the former without a listening socket; B requires the latter without per-client server launch. HTTP+SSE is the deprecated predecessor, not the default for a new current-revision integration.

distractorNotes.a: Loopback HTTP still needs a listening endpoint, violating A's explicit socket restriction.
distractorNotes.c: Legacy compatibility can justify supporting HTTP+SSE, but this scenario is a new current-revision deployment with no legacy-client requirement.
distractorNotes.d: A subprocess per remote client changes B's stated shared-service lifecycle rather than connecting to its independently operated endpoint.

sourceNote: Transports / Overview (stdio and Streamable HTTP as the standard bindings)

stem: A legacy MCP host remains pinned to revision 2025-06-18 while its replacement is built. It launches a repository-analysis server that needs project paths and requests occasional model completions. The architect must distinguish advisory coordination from enforced isolation and retain host control over model access during migration. Which two design decisions fit those boundaries? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Advertise the project directory through Roots and rely on that declaration instead of OS permissions to contain server file access.
Use Roots to communicate intended project scope, with OS permissions or sandboxing separately enforcing filesystem isolation.
Keep model credentials in the host but automatically honor the server's model preferences and completion requests after connection approval.
Mediate Sampling through the host's client, retaining approval, model-selection and usage controls rather than giving the server model access.
Expose a project resource URI and treat client permission to read it as enforcement of the server process's filesystem permissions.

explanation: Under protocol revision 2025-06-18, Roots and Sampling are the two client-side features that carry these controls. Roots let the client declare the filesystem directory boundaries and repository URIs a server is expected to operate within; the specification says servers SHOULD respect root boundaries, so Roots are a coordination mechanism rather than an enforced security boundary, and actual isolation must come from OS file permissions or sandboxing. Sampling routes any server-requested LLM completion through the client, so the client keeps control over model access, model selection, and permissions, and can apply spend limits and human approval before the request reaches a model. Note that both features were classified as Deprecated in protocol revision 2026-07-28 (SEP-2577) and become eligible for removal in the first revision released on or after 2027-07-28: new implementations should instead pass directories via tool parameters, resource URIs, or server configuration, and integrate directly with LLM provider APIs.

distractorNotes.a: Roots communicate intended scope; they do not constrain the server process's operating-system permissions.
distractorNotes.c: Keeping credentials in the host is useful, but automatically honoring server requests gives up the host's model-selection and approval decisions.
distractorNotes.e: A resource interface governs exposed context, not what the server's own process can read from the filesystem.

sourceNote: Understanding MCP clients / Core Client Features (Roots and Sampling)

stem: A Messages API assistant turn contains parallel calls to two independent client-side read tools and no pending server-tool calls. Both client-tool executions have completed, and the UI also has a new user clarification to send. The client must preserve the tool-call relationships without inserting an extra conversational turn between calls and results. Which two assembly decisions produce a valid continuation? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Return both results together in the immediately following user message, matching each result to its originating tool_use_id.
Return each result in its own user turn and request a model continuation between them so the faster tool can influence the response.
Place the clarification after the tool_result blocks in that user message, keeping the results first in its content array.
Put the new clarification before the result blocks in the same user message so the latest user intent has priority over tool data.
Combine both outputs into one result for the first call and describe the second call's outcome inside that result's text content.

explanation: The client must return a matching tool_result for each call together in the immediately following user message. Result blocks come before text in that message. With no pending server-tool calls, the new clarification may follow those results. If an unresolved server-tool call were present, the continuation would instead need to contain only client-tool results; the stem excludes that exception.

distractorNotes.b: The parallel calls belong to one assistant turn and need their matching results together before the next model continuation.
distractorNotes.d: Text may accompany tool results, but the result blocks must precede text in the content array.
distractorNotes.e: Each call needs its own matching result identity; describing a second output inside the first result leaves the second call unmatched.

sourceNote: Handle tool calls / Important formatting requirements

stem: A service agent has a stable policy prefix and frequently used tools that already cache well. It now needs occasional access to a large, pre-registered catalog of specialist tools. The team wants a small initial model context without rewriting the stable prefix whenever a specialist tool is discovered. Which integration design fits?

options.text: Load a small toolset initially, then rewrite its non-deferred top-level definitions whenever the application identifies a specialist operation.
Load the complete specialist catalog from the start and cache its definitions, treating reduced cache-read cost as reduced active context.
Defer specialist definitions behind tool search so discovered tools enter the conversation through tool references, leaving the cached prefix unchanged.
Start a fresh specialist-only conversation for each discovered tool and resend the policy prefix there, discarding the ongoing task history.

explanation: Deferred definitions do not enter the static prefix. Tool search adds discovered definitions through tool_reference blocks in conversation history, preserving the prefix used for prompt caching. The full matching definitions still belong in the request's tool catalog; deferral governs when they enter model context. Editing non-deferred definitions instead changes the tools prefix and invalidates later cache levels.

distractorNotes.a: Changing the non-deferred tools prefix invalidates its cache and the system and message caches after it.
distractorNotes.b: Caching changes repeated processing and billing; the complete loaded catalog still occupies the model's context.
distractorNotes.d: Fresh conversations with different tool prefixes do not preserve the existing conversation's cached prefix or its task history.

sourceNote: Tool use with prompt caching / defer_loading and cache preservation

stem: A codebase investigation has accumulated 120,000 tokens of file-reading results. Old file contents can be fetched again, but the model must retain which searches it performed and their original arguments. Recent results must remain available. The selected model supports server-side tool-result clearing. Which context policy best meets these requirements?

options.text: Compact the conversation into a summary at the threshold, replacing the original search calls and arguments with a narrative of the investigation.
Clear older tool-result contents at a threshold, retain recent results, and leave tool-input clearing disabled to preserve original calls and arguments.
Clear both old tool inputs and results at the threshold, relying on a persistent copy outside model context to reconstruct the investigation later.
Cache the accumulated tool history and keep it in each request, using cache hits rather than clearing to reduce the model's occupied context.

explanation: Tool-result clearing removes older result content and substitutes placeholders while retaining tool calls by default. The retention setting preserves recent results; leaving clear_tool_inputs false preserves the original calls and arguments. This reduces model context without summarizing those calls away. Clearing historical content can invalidate affected cached prefixes, so it is a context-capacity decision rather than a promise to preserve every cache hit.

distractorNotes.a: Compaction is useful for broader history reduction, but a narrative replacement does not preserve the original call-and-argument sequence required here.
distractorNotes.c: External retention can help recovery, but clearing inputs removes the original calls from the model's current context.
distractorNotes.d: Caching reduces repeated-prefix cost and processing; it does not remove historical tool content from the context window.

sourceNote: Context editing / Server-side strategies (Tool result clearing)

stem: An analyst agent fetches thousands of transactions, filters them, computes totals, and then looks up merchants for the remaining records. Each request needs different filters and conditional follow-up calls. The team wants to retain the existing reusable tools and avoid a new backend endpoint for each analysis while reducing model round trips and raw JSON in model context. Which design best fits?

options.text: Keep a conventional model-mediated loop and cache its transaction results, letting Claude inspect each full result before choosing the next tool.
Create a dedicated backend aggregation endpoint for each analysis pattern, maintaining its filters and merchant lookup conditions in application code.
Issue transaction and merchant lookup calls together before inspecting the transaction results, then send their raw outputs to one synthesis turn.
Let Claude write code that calls the existing tools programmatically, filters intermediate results, and returns the computed summary to model context.

explanation: Programmatic tool calling lets generated code orchestrate enabled tools, branch on results, and filter or aggregate data before returning output to Claude. Client tools still execute in the application; their results go back to the code execution environment rather than directly into model context. This supports request-specific analysis without a model turn for each transformation or a separately maintained endpoint for each pattern.

distractorNotes.a: Caching may reduce repeated processing, but the raw results still enter model context and the model still mediates each step.
distractorNotes.b: Backend aggregation can be effective for stable analyses, but per-pattern endpoints violate the stated maintainability constraint.
distractorNotes.c: Merchant lookups depend on the filtered transaction results; premature parallel calls do not resolve that dependency and still return raw data.

sourceNote: Programmatic tool calling / Architecture and latency reduction

stem: A real-time coding assistant uses Claude to generate a large configuration file through a file_writer tool. Standard tool streaming buffers each parameter value before emitting it, delaying the large file-content parameter. The team enables eager_input_streaming: true to receive fragments sooner. What input-handling design must the client use before executing the file-writing call?

options.text: The client receives tool input fragments immediately without server-side JSON validation, requiring client code to accumulate fragments and guard against partial JSON.
Treat content_block_stop as proof that the accumulated input is valid, then pass it directly to the file writer without guarding JSON parsing.
Execute the file writer when the first fragment parses successfully, then treat later fragments as additional calls that extend the initial file.
Parse each input_json_delta as an independent JSON object and merge the objects, discarding fragments that do not parse on their own.

explanation: Fine-grained tool streaming bypasses server-side buffering and JSON validation, reducing the wait for fragments of a large parameter. The client concatenates partial_json strings from input_json_delta events and guards parsing when the tool-use content block closes. Even the accumulated input can be invalid or incomplete, especially after truncation, so block completion alone is not proof of valid tool arguments. Unparseable input should be reported as a tool error rather than executed.

distractorNotes.b: The block-closing event is when the client attempts parsing, not a server validation guarantee. Fine-grained streaming can leave invalid accumulated input.
distractorNotes.c: A prefix that happens to parse does not establish that the tool's input is complete. Later fragments belong to the same call, not new file-writer invocations.
distractorNotes.d: Deltas contain string fragments of one JSON value and need concatenation. Individual fragments need not parse as complete objects.

sourceNote: Fine-grained tool streaming / Trade-offs and unbuffered JSON delivery

stem: A team has three integration contracts: (1) embed Claude Code's existing agent loop and file tools in a local Python application; (2) keep an existing application's custom tool-loop state machine as the owner of each model invocation; and (3) have Anthropic operate an agent loop and cloud sandbox for document audits. Which combination matches the required ownership boundaries?

options.text: Use the Agent SDK for the local application and custom state machine, then Managed Agents for hosted audits, standardizing the first two on its built-in loop.
Use the Agent SDK for the local application, direct Messages API calls for the existing state machine, and Managed Agents with a managed sandbox for hosted audits.
Use direct Messages API calls for the local application and custom state machine, then Managed Agents for hosted audits, implementing local file tools and the loop anew.
Use the Agent SDK for the local application, direct Messages API calls for the existing state machine, and deploy another Agent SDK process for the document audits.

explanation: The Agent SDK embeds Claude Code's capabilities and agent loop in a process the team operates. Direct API access lets the existing application retain its own tool loop rather than adopting that harness. Managed Agents provides an Anthropic-operated loop and can use an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox. These are ownership choices, not a claim that approval gates or observability are exclusive to a particular SDK.

distractorNotes.a: The Agent SDK supplies its own agent loop; adopting it for the second integration changes the required ownership of model invocations.
distractorNotes.c: Reimplementing local tools and the loop can work, but the first contract explicitly requires embedding Claude Code's existing capabilities.
distractorNotes.d: A separately deployed Agent SDK process remains infrastructure the team operates rather than the hosted loop and sandbox required for audits.

sourceNote: Agent SDK overview / Compare the Agent SDK to other Claude tools

stem: An MCP server offers a repeatable incident-review procedure. A user should explicitly launch the procedure from a menu; the host then attaches selected incident records, and the model may request diagnostic operations. The procedure itself should not be an action the model autonomously chooses. Which interface design best follows MCP's intended interaction models?

options.text: Expose the procedure as a tool with instructions to seek confirmation, attach records as resources, and expose diagnostics as tools.
Expose the procedure as a resource the host attaches on startup, attach incident records as resources, and expose diagnostics as tools.
Expose the procedure as a user-selected prompt, attach incident records as application-selected resources, and expose diagnostics as tools.
Expose the procedure as a user-selected prompt, attach records as resources, and encode diagnostic operations as additional prompt templates.

explanation: MCP's intended mapping is user-selected prompts for reusable procedures, application-driven resources for context, and model-requested tools for operations. It matches the three distinct initiation points in the scenario. Hosts retain discretion over interfaces and approval; the mapping does not mean tools bypass human oversight or that prompt templates themselves execute diagnostic operations.

distractorNotes.a: A confirmation-gated tool still makes the procedure available for model selection rather than providing the requested user-selected template.
distractorNotes.b: Automatic attachment supplies context but does not represent the explicit user launch of a reusable procedure.
distractorNotes.d: Additional prompt templates supply instructions; executable diagnostic operations need tool interfaces.

sourceNote: Server concepts / Tools, Resources and Prompts user interaction models

stem: An MCP host caches several telemetry resources whose URIs remain stable while their contents change. Polling each resource every five seconds creates avoidable traffic. Under revision 2026-07-28, the host needs change-driven cache invalidation followed by a fresh read when a watched resource changes. Which design fits without treating catalog changes as content changes?

options.text: Subscribe to resource-list changes and reread the cached resources when the server reports additions or removals from the resource catalog.
Subscribe to the watched resource URIs, use resource-updated notifications to invalidate their cached contents, and read those resources again.
Subscribe to the watched resource URIs and replace cached content directly from each resource-updated notification without a follow-up read.
Subscribe to resource-list changes and preserve cached content while each resource URI remains present in the unchanged resource catalog.

explanation: Resource subscriptions identify watched URIs through notifications.resourceSubscriptions in a subscriptions/listen request. A server advertising resource subscriptions sends notifications/resources/updated when watched content changes. The notification identifies the resource; the documented flow then reads updated contents with resources/read. Resource-list notifications instead concern changes to the catalog, which can remain unchanged while telemetry values change.

distractorNotes.a: A catalog notification does not track content changes to an existing resource with the same URI.
distractorNotes.c: The update notification identifies the changed URI rather than carrying replacement resource contents.
distractorNotes.d: Stable resource identity does not establish content freshness; the watched telemetry can change without catalog additions or removals.

sourceNote: Resources / Subscriptions (subscriptions/listen and notifications/resources/updated)

stem: An MCP server accepts a well-formed call to a known customer-lookup tool. The downstream CRM cannot find the supplied customer ID, and the lookup contract treats that outcome as a tool failure. The model should be able to correct the identifier without reconnecting to the server. Which error boundary should the adapter use?

options.text: Return a top-level JSON-RPC request error, classifying the unsuccessful CRM lookup in the same category as an unknown MCP tool.
Return a transport-level failure and let the client's reconnection policy retry the same lookup once the MCP connection is restored.
Return a successful tool result containing an empty customer object, keeping the tool's failure flag unset to preserve the success path.
Return a JSON-RPC result containing isError: true and a description of the failed lookup so the host can pass the failure to the model.

explanation: MCP distinguishes request/protocol problems, such as an unknown tool, from execution problems such as external API and business-logic failures. Here the MCP call was valid and the failure occurred during execution, so the server reports it inside a tool result with isError: true. Clients should provide execution errors to the model for recovery. A JSON-RPC error does not inherently mean that a transport must crash or disconnect.

distractorNotes.a: The request named a known tool and was well formed; classifying its business failure as a request-structure error uses the wrong boundary.
distractorNotes.b: Reconnecting addresses transport availability, not the supplied identifier that caused this lookup failure.
distractorNotes.c: The stated contract classifies a missing customer as failure, so an empty success object hides information needed for correction.

sourceNote: Tools / Error Handling (Protocol Errors vs Tool Execution Errors)

stem: A Contextual Retrieval job processes 10,000 contracts averaging 25,000 tokens each: 250 million source-document tokens before repeated per-chunk requests. Each contract produces many chunk-context requests that must retain the full contract for interpretation. Requests for one contract can run within the cache lifetime. Which layout and schedule best reuse that repeated input without changing what the contextualizer sees?

options.text: Keep the contract before the varying chunk, cache the contract prefix, and begin sibling chunk requests after the first response starts.
Keep the varying chunk before the contract, mark the end of the contract for caching, and group requests by contract to maximize reuse.
Keep the contract before the chunk and mark the end of each varying chunk for caching, relying on lookback to cache the contract itself.
Keep the contract before the varying chunk and cache the contract prefix, launching every chunk request before the first response begins.

explanation: A cache entry covers the exact prefix through its breakpoint. Keeping the shared contract before the changing chunk and marking the end of that shared prefix lets sibling requests reuse it. The cache becomes available after the first response begins, so that first request must get ahead of sibling requests. The 250 million tokens describe the source corpus, not total uncached input: including a contract once for each of its many chunks repeats its tokens.

distractorNotes.b: A changing chunk before the breakpoint changes the cumulative prefix, so identical contract text later in the request does not yield the intended hit.
distractorNotes.c: Lookback finds entries previously written at breakpoints; it does not create a contract-only entry behind a varying chunk breakpoint.
distractorNotes.d: A correct breakpoint is insufficient when sibling requests start before the first cache entry becomes available.

sourceNote: Structuring your prompt / Writes at breakpoints, exact prefixes and concurrent-request cache availability

stem: A stable 150,000-token runbook library fits the selected model's context window with room for instructions, questions and answers. Queries combine procedures across many sections. A cached full-context prototype already meets the team's measured accuracy, latency and cost targets. The team has little capacity to operate additional infrastructure and no near-term corpus growth requirement. Which production recommendation is best supported?

options.text: Build a hybrid RAG pipeline now and retire the prototype, using the smaller retrieved context as sufficient evidence of better end-to-end performance.
Build hierarchical retrieval and reranking before release to prepare for a larger corpus, even though current capacity and performance targets are met.
Deploy the validated cached full-context design, monitor its targets, and revisit retrieval if corpus size or measured requirements make it necessary.
Replace the library with a cached concise summary before release, using the smaller input footprint as sufficient evidence that operational details are retained.

explanation: The Contextual Retrieval article presents a full-knowledge-base prompt as a simple option when the material fits, with caching reducing repeated processing cost and latency. Here the scenario supplies the crucial evidence: the full-context design meets measured targets and infrastructure capacity is limited. That justifies deploying it, not claiming whole-context input is universally more accurate than RAG. Growth or changed evaluation results could justify retrieval later.

distractorNotes.a: Fewer input tokens do not establish better end-to-end results; a retrieval pipeline must also find the information the query needs.
distractorNotes.b: Hierarchical retrieval may become appropriate, but adding it now spends scarce operating capacity without a demonstrated unmet requirement.
distractorNotes.d: A summary reduces context but may omit required details; its smaller size is not a substitute for the prototype's measured task performance.

sourceNote: When to use RAG vs In-Context Retrieval with Prompt Caching

stem: A host temporarily supports existing MCP Sampling integrations under revision 2026-07-28 while planning migration from this deprecated feature. A third-party server requests nested completions and supplies model preferences. The host must retain control over what reaches the model and constrain usage rather than trusting server self-regulation. Which two controls belong at the host boundary? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Let the server select the model from its preferred list and enforce its own request budget, with host usage reports reviewed afterward.
Provide client-side review that lets users inspect, edit or deny sampling prompts before they are sent to the model.
Approve the server once at installation and rely on its prompt filter to reject sensitive content before each nested completion.
Apply client-side usage limits and make the final model selection in the host, treating server model preferences as advisory.
Review generated responses before returning them to the server, using that check in place of reviewing prompts before model invocation.

explanation: The MCP specification's sampling security considerations place the controls on the client, not the server: clients SHOULD implement user approval controls, with UI that lets users review, edit, and deny sampling requests before they reach a model, and SHOULD implement rate limiting. Because the client owns model access and selection, it is also the layer that can cap token spend and restrict which models a server may reach. Delegating either control to the server defeats the trust boundary, since the untrusted server is the party being constrained. Note that Sampling itself was classified as Deprecated in protocol revision 2026-07-28 (SEP-2577); the deprecated features registry records it as eligible for removal no earlier than the first revision released on or after 2027-07-28, and existing integrations should migrate to calling LLM provider APIs directly.

distractorNotes.a: Post-hoc reports do not enforce a usage limit, and server model hints do not override the client's final model-selection authority.
distractorNotes.c: Installation approval and server-side filtering do not retain client-side control over each prompt sent to the model.
distractorNotes.e: Response review is useful, but it occurs after the prompt has reached the model and usage has been incurred.

sourceNote: Sampling / User Interaction Model and Security Considerations

stem: A research service uses explicit prompt-cache breakpoints. Its 12 tool definitions and 5,000-token system policy are identical across cases; each case has a different conversation that grows through tool calls and results. Requests remain within the cache lifetime, and each turn adds fewer than 20 blocks. The design needs a reusable tools-plus-policy entry across cases and incremental history reuse within a case. Which two placements meet those goals within the four-breakpoint limit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Place a breakpoint at the end of the stable system policy, caching the preceding tools and the policy as one shared prefix.
Place a breakpoint at the end of the tool definitions and treat it as also covering the system policy that follows them.
Place a breakpoint on each of the 12 tool definitions so changes to individual tools leave the subsequent policy cache intact.
Move a breakpoint to the final eligible message block as the case progresses, allowing later turns to reuse prior history writes.
Keep a breakpoint on the first user message of each case instead of moving it forward, so accumulating history is cached implicitly.

explanation: The prefix order is tools, then system, then messages. A breakpoint at the end of the system policy therefore writes an entry covering both tools and policy, reusable across different case histories. A moving breakpoint at the final eligible message block writes the growing case prefix; later turns can find the previous write within the lookback window stated in the scenario. A breakpoint on the final tool caches tools, not system content that comes afterward.

distractorNotes.b: Cache entries end at the marked breakpoint; later system content is outside a final-tool entry.
distractorNotes.c: Twelve markers exceed the four-breakpoint limit, and changing an earlier tool changes the prefix for the later system policy.
distractorNotes.e: Writes stop at the breakpoint; keeping it on the first user message does not cache later tool calls and results.

sourceNote: Structuring your prompt / Multi-turn conversations and Tool caching
